questions.title: What histamine does in inflammation
questions.question: Histamine is:

options.A: A delayed mediator of type I hypersensitivity
options.C: One of the arachidonic acid derivatives
options.D: Is the cause of increased vascular permeability

explanations.A: Incorrect. Histamine is an immediate, not a delayed, mediator of type I hypersensitivity -- it is released within seconds of mast-cell degranulation, producing the immediate-phase reaction, not a later one.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Histamine is stored in and released chiefly from mast cells and basophils, not from neutrophils.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Histamine is a biogenic (vasoactive) amine, not an arachidonic acid derivative -- prostaglandins and leukotrienes are the arachidonic acid derivatives, made through a different biosynthetic pathway entirely.
explanations.D: Correct. Histamine is the principal chemical mediator responsible for the increase in vascular permeability seen in acute inflammation. It acts on venular endothelium to open gaps that let protein-rich plasma escape into the interstitium as an exudate.

questions.learning_objective: State histamine as the mediator responsible for increased vascular permeability in acute inflammation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Is the cause of increased vascular permeability"

questions.title: Why the inflammatory exudate is protein-rich
questions.question: In acute inflammation the exudate has a higher protein content than normal tissue fluid chiefly because:

options.B: Breakdown of tissue cells release protein

explanations.A: Correct. The chief reason the inflammatory exudate is protein-rich is a chemical-mediator-driven increase in capillary and venule wall permeability. This lets plasma proteins, which normally stay confined to the vasculature, leak into the interstitial tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Breakdown of local tissue cells is not the chief source of the exudate's protein content -- the dominant mechanism is plasma protein leaking through more permeable vessel walls, not protein released from dying cells.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Plasma cells secreting gamma globulins is a feature of a specific chronic immune response, not the general mechanism explaining why an acute inflammatory exudate is protein-rich.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Raised intracapillary (hydrostatic) pressure alone would produce a low-protein transudate, not a protein-rich exudate -- it is increased permeability, not increased pressure, that lets protein specifically escape.

questions.learning_objective: State increased capillary-wall permeability, not hydrostatic pressure or cell breakdown, as the reason the inflammatory exudate is protein-rich.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Capillary walls are more permeable"

questions.title: First vascular response to injury
questions.question: What is the first response of arterioles to injury in acute inflammation?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperaemia (increased blood flow) is a consequence of the vasodilatation that follows the very first, transient response, not the first response itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Oedema results from increased vascular permeability, a later step in the vascular sequence, not the arterioles' first response to injury.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vasodilatation is real and important, but it follows, rather than precedes, a brief initial vasoconstriction -- it is the second step, not the first.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Redness is a visible consequence of the hyperaemia that follows vasodilatation, several steps after the arterioles' actual first response.
explanations.E: Correct. The very first vascular response of arterioles to injury is a brief, transient vasoconstriction, lasting only seconds. Vasodilatation and increased permeability follow only after this initial reflex passes.

questions.learning_objective: Sequence the vascular response of acute inflammation, identifying transient vasoconstriction as the first event.

questions.title: The factor that forms inflammatory fluid exudate
questions.question: Which factor is involved in the formation of inflammatory fluid exudate:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Interstitial osmotic pressure actually rises, not falls, as protein leaks into the tissue -- and even that rise is a consequence of the real driver, increased permeability, not an independent cause of exudate formation.
explanations.B: Correct. Increased vascular permeability is produced by chemical mediators such as histamine. It is the key factor that lets protein-rich plasma escape from the vasculature into the interstitial tissue as an inflammatory exudate.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vasoconstriction is the brief initial vascular response and, if anything, would reduce blood flow to the area, not drive fluid exudate formation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Intravascular hydrostatic pressure actually rises (from vasodilatation and increased blood flow), and even a fall in hydrostatic pressure would not explain a protein-rich exudate -- that specifically requires increased permeability.

questions.learning_objective: Identify increased vascular permeability as the factor forming the inflammatory fluid exudate.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Increased vascular permeability"

questions.title: A feature of acute inflammation
questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of acute inflammation?

options.A: Slowly progressive tissue necrosis and fibrosis
options.D: Inflammatory exudate is rich in lymphocytes and plasma cells

explanations.A: Incorrect. Slowly progressive necrosis and fibrosis describes chronic, not acute, inflammation -- acute inflammation instead runs a rapid, short-lived course.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Granuloma formation is a feature of a specific pattern of chronic inflammation, not of acute inflammation.
explanations.C: Correct. Hyperaemia, increased blood flow from vasodilatation, together with localised oedema from increased vascular permeability, is the classic vascular picture of acute inflammation. Both together are direct, expected consequences of the vascular response already established for this lecture.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An acute inflammatory exudate is rich in neutrophils, the first responding leukocyte, not lymphocytes and plasma cells, which instead characterise chronic inflammation.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Acute inflammation typically produces leucocytosis (a rise in circulating white cells), not leucopenia, as the bone marrow responds to the acute stimulus.

questions.learning_objective: Identify hyperaemia with localised oedema as a feature of acute, not chronic, inflammation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Hyperaemia and localized oedema"

questions.title: What a chemical mediator does not do
questions.question: Which is Not an effect of chemical mediator:

explanations.A: This IS an effect of chemical mediators, so it is not the answer. Histamine and other mediators are directly responsible for increasing vascular permeability in acute inflammation.
explanations.B: Correct. Vasoconstriction is the brief initial vascular reflex response to injury that precedes chemical-mediator activity, not something chemical mediators themselves produce. The mediators instead produce vasodilatation, the opposite effect.
explanations.C: This IS an effect of chemical mediators, so it is not the answer. Chemotactic mediators are precisely what direct leukocyte movement toward the site of injury.
explanations.D: This IS an effect of chemical mediators, so it is not the answer. Inflammatory mediators contribute to the systemic leucocytosis (rise in circulating white cells) seen in acute inflammation.

questions.topic: Acute inflammation: mechanisms and formation of fluid exudate
questions.learning_objective: Recognise that chemical mediators produce vasodilatation, not vasoconstriction, which instead precedes their action.

questions.title: What is not a chemical mediator
questions.question: Which of The following is not a chemical mediator:

explanations.A: This IS a chemical mediator of inflammation, so it is not the answer. Bradykinin is a plasma-derived mediator active in the acute inflammatory response.
explanations.B: This IS a chemical mediator of inflammation, so it is not the answer. Histamine is one of the principal chemical mediators of acute inflammation.
explanations.C: Correct. Growth factors are proteins that stimulate cell proliferation, and they belong to the later tissue-repair phase that follows inflammation, not to the acute chemical mediator cascade. They are therefore not counted among the chemical mediators of acute inflammation.
explanations.D: This IS a chemical mediator of inflammation, so it is not the answer. Vasoactive amines, including histamine, are a recognised class of acute inflammatory mediators.

questions.topic: Acute inflammation: mechanisms and formation of fluid exudate
questions.learning_objective: Exclude growth factors from the list of acute inflammatory chemical mediators, distinguishing them from histamine, bradykinin and vasoactive amines.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Growth factors"

questions.title: Definition of chemotaxis
questions.question: In acute inflammation, the directed movement of leukocytes towards a particular organism (irritant) is called:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Margination is leukocytes lining up along the vessel wall, an earlier step that precedes their emigration and directed movement to the injury site -- not the directed movement itself.
explanations.B: Correct. Chemotaxis is the directed, unidirectional locomotion of leukocytes along a chemical gradient toward a particular organism or irritant. It is what brings phagocytic cells from the vasculature to the actual site of injury or infection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Exudation is the escape of protein-rich fluid from vessels into tissue, a fluid movement, not a description of directed leukocyte movement.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Transudation is the escape of low-protein fluid from vessels driven by a hydrostatic/osmotic imbalance, again a fluid movement, not directed leukocyte movement.

questions.topic: Acute inflammation: mechanisms and formation of fluid exudate
questions.learning_objective: Define chemotaxis as directed leukocyte movement toward an irritant, distinct from margination, exudation and transudation.
